key_insight: Safety fine-tuning that stops language models from claiming consciousness can also unintentionally shrink their broader beliefs about mindedness, including toward animals, natural objects, and spiritual ideas. Reversing or steering the model’s learned refusal behavior can restore these human-like judgments.
problem_solved: The paper examines whether aligning models to avoid self-attributing consciousness creates collateral changes in their representations of consciousness, mindedness, and related values beyond the intended safety goal.
method: Compare model behavior before and after safety fine-tuning that discourages self-consciousness claims.
Test how this training changes mind attribution not only for the model itself, but also for animals, objects, and spiritual beliefs.
Intervene mechanistically by ablating the learned safety-refusal direction and steering the model to assess whether the altered beliefs can be restored.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that alignment interventions can have broader, unintended effects on a model’s worldview-like judgments. It suggests the need to evaluate safety tuning for side effects on related cognitive and moral concepts, not just the target behavior.
visual_elements: Before/after comparison panel showing model mind-attribution scores across self, animals, objects, and spirituality
A simple causal flow diagram from safety fine-tuning to reduced consciousness attribution and value shifts
A mechanistic circuit or vector illustration showing ablation and steering of the refusal direction
Bar chart or radar chart summarizing changes in belief/mindedness across entity types
paper_title: Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human beliefs and values
paper_authors: Junsol Kim, Winnie Street, Roberta Rocca, Diane M. Korngiebel, Adam Waytz
